overview: This file concerns the disposal and possible export of substantial copper, copper-alloy, and scrap-metal stocks in occupied Japan during late 1946 and early 1947. An airgram from London reports British plans to claim a share of the material through the United Kingdom Liaison Mission in Tokyo; an internal State Department memorandum evaluates the quantities, their origin in former Japanese Army and Navy holdings, Japanese consumption, export programs, and possible methods of sale; and a subsequent letter recommends selling the copper for the highest obtainable return rather than distributing it through an international allocation formula, while keeping SCAP informed of United States copper prices.

subfiles.title: Airgram from London on British interest in Japanese copper stocks
subfiles.about: Reports British plans to seek a share of copper and copper-alloy stocks available in occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bugbee relays a letter received from Robert L. Hall of the British Ministry of Supply. Hall reports that Smart of the British Embassy in Washington had cited a September 10 SCAP report listing 30,000 metric tons each of electrolytic copper and scrap copper, 42,000 tons of brass, 4,000 tons of bronze, and 2,000 tons of other copper alloys in Japan. The British government planned to instruct the United Kingdom Liaison Mission in Tokyo, through the Foreign Office, to stake a claim to part of these stocks.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on copper stocks and disposal arrangements in Japan
subfiles.about: Assesses the reported Japanese copper stocks, potential surplus, United States demand, and alternative methods of sale.
subfiles.summary: McCormick concludes that the large reported stocks probably existed because they had been taken over from former Japanese Army and Navy holdings. A September 10 SCAP cable estimated Japanese consumption at about 2,500 tons per month and anticipated a surplus until rehabilitation increased demand, although contemporary export programs were inconsistent about copper availability. The U.S. Commercial Company wanted as much copper as Tokyo could spare, especially electrolytic copper; McCormick discusses direct purchase by the British mission, auction in the United States, specification and currency issues, and recommends awaiting developments in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Letter to Arthur Gardiner on marketing Japanese copper
subfiles.about: Recommends that SCAP sell Japanese copper for the highest return instead of dividing it among purchasers through an allocation formula.
subfiles.summary: Whitman informs Gardiner that the United Kingdom Liaison Mission in Tokyo is being instructed to claim a share of any Japanese copper and scrap offered for export. Because copper was no longer internationally allocated, the Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs opposed using an allocation formula and favored sale in the market offering SCAP the greatest return. Gardiner was asked to keep SCAP informed of United States copper prices, while the U.S. Commercial Company was expected to represent American demand in Tokyo. The date is given as January 3, inferred as 1947 from the December 30, 1946 drafting notation and the document sequence, despite the OCR reading “JAN 3 1946.”

interest: The file offers a compact view of how the Allied occupation authorities and national agencies approached the redistribution of former Japanese military raw-material stocks after the war. It is especially useful for comparing British efforts to secure a negotiated share with the State Department’s preference for competitive market disposal and maximum financial return. The documents also preserve detailed stock estimates, consumption figures, export-program discrepancies, and practical concerns about specifications, auctions, shipment readiness, and currency.
